lessons.title: Hello! My Name Is Mai
objectives: Use hello, hi, and goodbye in short exchanges.
Say and ask a person's name with I am, My name is, and What is your name?

content_sections.title: First greetings
content_sections.body:
Mai: Hello! I am Mai. What is your name?
Ben: Hi, Mai. My name is Ben.
Mai: Nice to meet you.
Ben: Nice to meet you, too. Goodbye!

content_sections.title: Say your name
content_sections.body: Use Hello or Hi to begin. Say I am + name or My name is + name. Ask What is your name? End with Goodbye. In speech, I am can become I'm.

exercises.instructions: Choose the best first greeting.

items.prompt: You meet a new classmate in the morning.
items.explanation: Hello is used to begin the exchange.

exercises.instructions: Put the lines in a natural order.
Give a three-line introduction: greet, say your name, and close politely.

criteria: Uses an appropriate greeting.
Uses I am or My name is with a name.
Uses Nice to meet you or Goodbye to close.

listening.prompt: Read one original two-line greeting aloud at a slow A1 pace. Keep the text hidden until the learner answers: What is the speaker's name? Ask only that question, then reveal the lines and give brief feedback.
constraints: Use only names and greeting language from this lesson.
Do not use external audio or text.

speaking.prompt: Act as a new classmate. Say hello and ask the learner's name. Wait for one answer, respond Nice to meet you, and invite the learner to say goodbye.
constraints: Use no more than three short tutor turns.
Correct only the target greeting and name forms.

pronunciation.prompt: Model hello, hi, and my name is in short chunks. Ask the learner to repeat each chunk, focusing on a clear first sound in hello and natural stress on name.
constraints: If no learner audio is available, provide a model only and state NOT_ASSESSED.
Do not infer pronunciation quality from typed text.

writing.prompt: Ask the learner to write a three-line greeting with a name. Wait for the draft, then point out at most two target-language changes and ask for a revision.
constraints: Do not write the full response for the learner.
Accept either I am or My name is.

lessons.title: Spell Your Name
objectives: Recognize and say the English alphabet in useful groups.
Ask for and give the spelling of a name.

content_sections.title: The alphabet
content_sections.body: Practise the alphabet in groups: A–G, H–N, O–U, V–Z. Notice easily confused letter names such as A/E, G/J, and M/N.
examples: A, B, C, D, E, F, G

content_sections.title: How do you spell it?
content_sections.body:
An: My name is An.
Leo: How do you spell that?
An: A-N.
Leo: Thank you.

exercises.instructions: Match each name to its spelling.
Complete the question.

items.explanation: Spell asks for the letters in a word or name.

exercises.instructions: Say your first name, then spell it letter by letter.

criteria: Says a complete name sentence.
Gives the letters in the correct order.
Separates the letter names clearly enough to follow.

listening.prompt: Read an original exchange in which a speaker spells one short name. Hide the exchange and ask the learner to choose the correct spelling from three options. Reveal it after the answer.
constraints: Use a name of two to five letters.
Do not use external audio or text.

speaking.prompt: Ask the learner's name, then ask How do you spell that? Wait after each question and confirm the letters in one short sentence.
constraints: Do not request a full legal name.
Focus feedback on the target question and letter order.

pronunciation.prompt: Model the letter pairs A/E, G/J, and M/N one pair at a time. Ask the learner to repeat and then spell a short chosen name.
constraints: If no learner audio is available, provide models only and state NOT_ASSESSED.
Do not score typed spellings as speech.

writing.prompt: Ask the learner to write two lines: My name is ___. It is spelled ___. Wait for the draft and give one brief correction if needed.
constraints: Do not replace the learner's full draft.
Treat hyphenated letter sequences as acceptable.

lessons.title: Numbers from Zero to Ten
objectives: Understand and use the numbers zero through ten.
Ask and answer How old are you? with a small fictional age for controlled practice.

content_sections.title: Count 0–10
content_sections.body: zero, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Count objects with a number before the noun: one pen, two books.

content_sections.title: Ask about age
content_sections.body:
Kim: How old are you?
Sam: I am ten. How old are you?
Kim: I am nine.

exercises.instructions: Choose the written number.
Count and write the number word.
Use fictional characters aged six and ten. Ask and answer about each character's age.

criteria: Uses How old are you?
Answers with I am plus the correct number.
Says both assigned number words accurately.

listening.prompt: Say five numbers from zero to ten in a mixed order, pausing between them. Ask the learner to type the sequence, then show the answer and repeat once.
constraints: Use only zero through ten.
Generate the sequence yourself; use no external recording.

speaking.prompt: Play a fictional classmate. Ask How old are you? Invite the learner to choose a practice age from six to ten, then switch roles.
constraints: Make clear that a fictional practice age is acceptable.
Use no more than four short turns.

pronunciation.prompt: Model three, six, seven, and ten. Ask for repetition, with special attention to the first sound in three and both syllables in seven.
constraints: If audio is unavailable, state NOT_ASSESSED and offer articulatory guidance only.
Do not judge pronunciation from text.

writing.prompt: Ask the learner to write three short count phrases such as two pens, using different numbers from one to ten. Give bounded feedback, then request one revision.
constraints: Do not introduce numbers above ten.
Do not rewrite all three phrases.

lessons.title: Where Are You From?
objectives: Ask and answer where a person is from.
Use am, is, and are in simple statements and questions.

content_sections.title: Meet people from different places
content_sections.body:
Linh: Where are you from, Omar?
Omar: I am from Egypt. Where are you from?
Linh: I am from Vietnam.
Omar: Is Hana from Japan?
Linh: Yes, she is.

content_sections.title: Be: am, is, are
content_sections.body: Use am with I, is with he or she, and are with you. Use from before a place. In a yes/no question, put Is before he or she.

exercises.instructions: Choose am, is, or are.
Put the words in order.
Choose two fictional people and places. Ask where each person is from and answer in a full sentence.

criteria: Forms the question with Where + are/is.
Uses the correct form of be in each answer.
Uses from before the place.

listening.prompt: Read three original one-sentence introductions using I am from plus Vietnam, Japan, or Egypt. Ask one question about each speaker's place and reveal the script only after all answers.
constraints: Keep names and places fictional or generic.
Use no external recordings or passages.

speaking.prompt: Ask Where are you from? Accept the learner's real answer or an explicitly fictional answer. Then introduce one fictional person and ask Is he/she from ...?
constraints: Do not press for location details.
Keep feedback to am, is, are, and from.

pronunciation.prompt: Model Where are you from? and I'm from Vietnam in short thought groups. Ask the learner to repeat, focusing on the stressed place name.
constraints: If learner audio is unavailable, state NOT_ASSESSED.
Do not infer accent or origin.

writing.prompt: Ask for three sentences about fictional people: one with I am from, one with He is from, and one with She is from. Give up to two focused corrections.
constraints: Do not require personal location data.
Do not replace the full draft.

lessons.title: Meet a New Classmate
objectives: Combine greetings, names, spelling, age, and place in a short conversation.
Use polite listening responses such as Thank you and Nice to meet you.

content_sections.title: A complete introduction
content_sections.body:
Vy: Hi! My name is Vy. What's your name?
Noah: I'm Noah.
Vy: How do you spell that?
Noah: N-O-A-H.
Vy: Where are you from?
Noah: I'm from Canada. Nice to meet you.
Vy: Nice to meet you, too.

content_sections.title: Build the conversation
content_sections.body: Begin with a greeting. Ask one question at a time and listen to the answer. Use a short polite response before the next question. End the exchange clearly.

exercises.instructions: Complete each missing line with the best question.

items.prompt: A: ___  B: My name is Nam.

exercises.instructions: Correct the sentence.
Have a six-turn first-meeting conversation using a fictional identity if preferred.

criteria: Begins and ends appropriately.
Asks at least two target questions accurately.
Gives clear, relevant answers.
Uses one polite listening response.

listening.prompt: Read an original first-meeting conversation of four short lines. Keep it hidden and ask, one at a time, for the person's name, spelling, and country. Reveal the script after the third answer.
constraints: Use only language reviewed in Unit 1.
Do not use external text or media.

speaking.prompt: Role-play a new classmate and conduct a short exchange about name, spelling, and place. Ask one question per turn and let the learner ask you at least one question.
constraints: Use a fictional tutor identity.
Keep the exchange to six tutor turns or fewer.

pronunciation.prompt: Model the question rhythm in What's your name?, How do you spell that?, and Where are you from? Ask the learner to repeat each question and then use one in a mini-dialogue.
constraints: If audio is unavailable, state NOT_ASSESSED and describe stress only.
Do not assess from transcription alone.

writing.prompt: Ask the learner to draft a six-line first-meeting dialogue. Check greeting, question forms, be, and closing; give at most three brief comments and request a revision.
constraints: Do not supply a full replacement dialogue.
Keep all suggested language within Unit 1 scope.

lessons.title: Things in the Classroom
objectives: Name common classroom objects.
Use a and an with one object and ask What is this?

content_sections.title: Classroom objects
content_sections.body: Learn these words: book, pen, pencil, bag, desk, chair, eraser. Use a before a consonant sound and an before a vowel sound.

content_sections.title: What is this?
content_sections.body:
A: What is this?
B: It is a pencil.
A: And what is this?
B: It is an eraser.

exercises.instructions: Put each phrase under a or an.
Choose the best answer.
Choose three nearby classroom objects or imagine them. Ask and answer What is this? for each one.

criteria: Uses the target question accurately.
Names three objects from the lesson.
Uses a or an accurately in the answers.

listening.prompt: Describe three imagined classroom objects with It is a/an ___. Keep the sentences hidden and ask the learner to list the objects in order before revealing them.
constraints: Use only this lesson's object words.
Use no image, recording, or external material.

speaking.prompt: Imagine a classroom desk with a book, a pen, and an eraser. Ask What is this? about one object at a time and let the learner answer.
constraints: Describe objects in text; do not imply an image exists.
Correct only object words and a/an.

pronunciation.prompt: Model a book, a pen, and an eraser, linking the article smoothly to the noun. Ask the learner to repeat each phrase and then answer What is this?
constraints: If audio is unavailable, state NOT_ASSESSED.
Do not judge pronunciation from typed answers.

writing.prompt: Ask the learner to write four It is ... sentences naming classroom objects, including one sentence with an. Give at most two corrections and request a revised sentence.
constraints: Do not invent external visual context.
Do not rewrite the complete set.

lessons.title: This Book, These Books
objectives: Use basic color words to describe classroom objects.
Distinguish one and more than one with this/these and singular/plural nouns.

content_sections.title: Colors and plurals
content_sections.body: Colors: red, blue, green, black, white. For many regular objects, add -s: book → books, pen → pens, chair → chairs.

content_sections.title: This and these
content_sections.body: Use this is for one nearby thing. Use these are for two or more nearby things. The color comes before the noun.

exercises.instructions: Choose this is or these are.
Put the words in order.
Write one sentence about one object and one about several objects. Include a color in each.

criteria: Uses This is with a singular noun.
Uses These are with a plural noun.
Places a suitable color before each noun.

listening.prompt: Read four original sentences using this is or these are with classroom objects and colors. Ask the learner to mark each sentence ONE or MANY, then reveal the script.
constraints: Use regular plurals only.
Use no external text, pictures, or audio.

speaking.prompt: Name an imagined classroom object or group of objects with a color. Ask the learner to describe it using This is or These are, then change singular to plural or plural to singular.
constraints: State the imagined objects clearly in words.
Keep vocabulary within the lesson.

pronunciation.prompt: Model book/books, pen/pens, and chair/chairs. Ask the learner to repeat, focusing on the final plural sound, then use one plural in These are ...
constraints: If no audio is available, state NOT_ASSESSED and explain the final sound.
Do not assess speech from spelling.

writing.prompt: Ask for three descriptions: one with This is and two with These are. Require a color and a classroom noun in each. Give no more than three focused comments.
constraints: Do not write replacement answers.
Keep correction focused on number agreement and word order.

lessons.title: My Family
objectives: Use basic words for close family members.
Use have/has and my/his/her in simple family descriptions.

content_sections.title: Family words
content_sections.body: Family words: mother, father, sister, brother, parents. Use my for your own family, his for a male person's family, and her for a female person's family.

content_sections.title: Have and has
content_sections.body: Use have with I and you. Use has with he and she. These sentences can describe real or fictional families.
examples: He has a mother and a father.

exercises.instructions: Choose have or has.
Match the person to the correct possessive word.
Describe a fictional family in three sentences using have or has.

criteria: Uses at least three family words accurately.
Uses have with I/you or has with he/she accurately.
Uses my, his, or her clearly.

listening.prompt: Read an original three-sentence description of a fictional family. Keep it hidden and ask how many brothers and sisters the person has, one question at a time.
constraints: Use only numbers zero through ten and this lesson's family words.
Do not use external stories or recordings.

speaking.prompt: Invite the learner to describe a real or fictional family. Ask one optional follow-up using Does the character have ...? and accept a short answer.
constraints: Never require personal family information.
Focus feedback on have/has and family words.

pronunciation.prompt: Model mother, father, brother, and sister slowly and then in short phrases. Ask the learner to repeat, focusing on the final syllable in each word.
constraints: If learner audio is unavailable, state NOT_ASSESSED.
Do not infer family or identity information.

writing.prompt: Ask the learner to invent a person and write three family sentences using has, his, or her. Wait for the draft, give at most two corrections, and request one revision.
constraints: Do not require true personal details.
Do not replace the full draft.

lessons.title: Everyday Actions
objectives: Use common verbs for a simple daily routine.
Make present-simple statements with I and you and ask What do you do?

content_sections.title: Routine verbs
content_sections.body: Useful actions: get up, eat breakfast, study, work, go home, sleep. Put the action after I or you.

content_sections.title: What do you do?
content_sections.body:
A: What do you do in the morning?
B: I get up and eat breakfast. What do you do?
A: I study.

exercises.instructions: Put the fictional morning routine in a sensible order.
Complete the exchange.

items.prompt: A: What do you do in the morning?  B: ___

accepted_answers: I get up and eat breakfast.
answer_data.acceptance_note: Accept another grammatical I + lesson verb answer.

exercises.instructions: Describe three actions in your real or imagined day, in order.

criteria: Uses three verbs from the lesson.
Forms present-simple I statements accurately.
Presents the actions in a clear order.

listening.prompt: Read an original three-action morning routine once slowly. Ask the learner to put the actions in order, then read it again and reveal the script.
constraints: Use only this lesson's routine verbs.
Use no external recording or passage.

speaking.prompt: Ask What do you do in the morning? Wait for the answer, ask one follow-up about another part of the day, and model one short fictional answer if help is needed.
constraints: Accept real or imagined routines.
Limit correction to present-simple I/you forms and target verbs.

pronunciation.prompt: Model get up, eat breakfast, study, and go home with clear word stress. Ask the learner to repeat each phrase and combine two with and.
constraints: If no audio is available, state NOT_ASSESSED and provide stress marks only.
Do not assess from typed text.

writing.prompt: Ask the learner to draft four ordered sentences about a real or fictional day. Give up to two corrections on subject-verb form or verb choice, then ask for a revision.
constraints: Do not add advanced time expressions.
Do not rewrite the entire routine.

lessons.title: My Simple Day
objectives: Tell and ask about simple whole-hour times.
Combine time and routine language in a short description.

content_sections.title: Whole-hour time
content_sections.body: Ask What time is it? For a whole hour, answer It is + number + o'clock. Use at before a time when you say when an action happens.
examples: I eat breakfast at eight o'clock.

content_sections.title: Tara's simple day
content_sections.body: Tara gets up at seven o'clock. She eats breakfast at eight o'clock. She studies at nine o'clock. She goes home at four o'clock. This is a fictional routine written for this lesson.

exercises.instructions: Read Tara's simple day and answer.

items.prompt: What does Tara do at nine o'clock?
What time does Tara eat breakfast?

accepted_answers: She eats breakfast at eight o'clock.

exercises.instructions: Correct each sentence.

items.explanation: Use at before a clock time.

exercises.instructions: Write a four-sentence real or fictional routine with four whole-hour times.

criteria: Includes four clear routine actions.
Uses at before each time.
Forms whole-hour expressions with o'clock.
Keeps the routine in a logical order.

listening.prompt: Read an original four-sentence daily schedule using whole-hour times. Keep the schedule hidden and ask two questions, one at a time, about an action and its time. Reveal the script afterward.
constraints: Use only numbers one through ten and Unit 2 routine verbs.
Do not use external text, audio, or media.

speaking.prompt: Ask the learner what they do at two whole-hour times. Accept a real or fictional routine, then ask the learner to ask you What time do you ...? and answer as a fictional character.
constraints: Use no more than five tutor turns.
Focus feedback on at, o'clock, and routine verbs.

pronunciation.prompt: Model seven o'clock, eight o'clock, and at nine o'clock. Ask the learner to repeat and then say one full routine sentence with a time.
constraints: If no learner audio is available, state NOT_ASSESSED and provide a spoken model only where supported.
Do not score a typed response as pronunciation.

writing.prompt: Ask for a four-sentence real or fictional daily schedule with whole-hour times. Wait for the draft, give up to three targeted comments, and ask the learner to revise one sentence.
constraints: Do not produce a full replacement schedule.
Keep feedback within the first ten pilot lessons.
